column4: This is the section's quoted command: Musa must remind his people of “the days of Allah” (أَيَّامَ اللَّهِ), the exact yawm wording whose gloss includes punishment and pardon.
This is the rescue-and-provision scene immediately before 20:81: Israel is saved from its enemy and given manna and quail, so the warning about transgression follows a concrete gift.

The verse joins provision (رَزَقْنَاكُمْ) to the command not to transgress and the warning “My anger may come upon you” (فَيَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبِي); it makes the two descents in the section a single conditional scene.
After the fall named in 20:81, God promises abundant forgiveness to the one who repents, believes, acts well, and is guided (ثُمَّ اهْتَدَىٰ); this is the passage's stated path out of the warning.

Musa returns to his people “angry and grieving” (غَضْبَانَ أَسِفًا) after the calf episode, then asks if they wanted their Lord's anger to come upon them; anger is both bodily stance and threatened descent here.

In the wilderness, God shades Israel with cloud and sends manna and quail, then tells them to eat from the good provision; this is another direct provision scene behind 20:81's gift-and-warning pattern.
After the command to enter and ask forgiveness in 2:58, the wrongdoers are struck by punishment from heaven; the verse gives the descent that follows refusal of a given way.

Israel asks for other food after the manna, and the verse says humiliation was laid upon them and they incurred anger from God (بَاءُوا بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ); it closely joins rejected provision, abasement, and anger.
This parallel wilderness account again names cloud, manna, quail, and provision from God; it makes the gift that precedes the warning in the section concrete.
Israel is told to enter the town, eat freely, and enter the gate prostrating while asking forgiveness; the verse places a path of submission and pardon beside the provision scene.
After the people alter the command in 7:161, punishment is sent down on the wrongdoers; the reversal makes the gift, instruction, and adverse outcome a connected sequence.
After recognizing that they had gone astray over the calf, the people fear loss unless God shows mercy; the verse links lost direction with the possibility of mercy in the same episode as 7:150–153.
Musa returns to his people angry and sorrowful, just as 20:86 does; the episode gives the section's bodily and spoken form of anger in a second account.
Musa asks God to forgive him and his brother and admit them into mercy; this is the pardon side of the calf episode's anger-and-humiliation outcome.
The calf-makers are promised anger from their Lord and humiliation (غَضَبٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ وَذِلَّةٌ); the verse directly stages anger reaching a group and a bodily/social abasement.
Those who do wrong and then repent and believe find their Lord forgiving and merciful; this continuation sets return and pardon against the prior calf judgment.
Musa's next words specify the remembrance commanded in 14:5: God saved Israel from Pharaoh's people, naming deliverance as a favor within these “days.”
The following verse makes gratitude lead to increase and ingratitude meet severe punishment; it connects bestowed favor with the opposite outcome that structures the section.
The verse names people God has cursed and become angry with (غَضِبَ عَلَيْهِ), then says they are farther from the even way; it joins anger to the lost-path side of the image.
The verse contrasts following God's pleasure (رِضْوَانَ اللَّهِ) with returning with His displeasure (بِسَخَطٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ); the section's lexicon explicitly calls anger the opposite of riḍā.
This verse promises guidance to a straight path immediately before 4:69 names the people God has favored; it makes the “way” of the favored companions explicit.

The verse names those God favored—prophets, truthful ones, martyrs, and the righteous—and ends by calling them good companions; it directly supports the section's reading of the favored path as a shared walk.
Those God favored, guided, and chose fall down prostrating and weeping; this is the section's exact link between bestowed favor, guidance, and a visible bodily response.
“Faces that day” are described as humbled (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ خَاشِعَةٌ); the verse supplies one side of the paired faces the section sets against نعمة.
The opposite faces on that day are called blissful/softened (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَاعِمَةٌ), from the same ن ع م root as the section's أَنْعَمْتَ; it makes the root's bodily sense visible.
The blissful face is pleased with its striving (لِسَعْيِهَا رَاضِيَةٌ); this connects the section's favor-and-pleasure contrast to the person's own work.
The righteous' faces display “the radiance of bliss” (نَضْرَةَ النَّعِيمِ); the verse directly extends the section's claim that favor leaves a recognizable mark on the face.
Some faces that day are radiant (مُسْفِرَةٌ), beginning the paired facial scene the section uses for the two groups.
Those radiant faces laugh and rejoice (ضَاحِكَةٌ مُسْتَبْشِرَةٌ); the verse specifies the expression of the favored side of the facial contrast.
Other faces that day have dust upon them (عَلَيْهَا غَبَرَةٌ); the “upon” construction closely matches the section's attention to what settles on a face.
A darkening covers those faces (تَرْهَقُهَا قَتَرَةٌ); this completes the image of a mark laid over the face, opposite the radiance in 80:38–39.
At judgment some faces whiten and others blacken (تَبْيَضُّ وُجُوهٌ وَتَسْوَدُّ وُجُوهٌ); this is a direct alternative account of judgment appearing in two faces.
The whitened faces are in God's mercy; the verse identifies the favorable meaning of the facial sign introduced in 3:106.
Those who do good receive the best and more, and neither dust nor abasement covers their faces (قَتَرٌ وَلَا ذِلَّةٌ); the verse makes the unmarked face a sign of the favorable outcome.
Those who earn evil have faces as if covered by pieces of dark night; the verse supplies the opposite facial outcome to 10:26 and to the section's softened face.
The Fire scorches the faces of its people (تَلْفَحُ وُجُوهَهُمُ النَّارُ), who grimace; this is a direct bodily reversal of the cool, softened face in the section.
Some faces on that day are radiant and looking toward their Lord; this is another explicit scene of a favorable face at judgment.
The radiant faces of 75:22 look toward their Lord (إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ); it makes their appearance a stance of hopeful encounter, alongside the section's رضا.
Other faces that day are gloomy (بَاسِرَةٌ); the verse gives the opposite expression to the radiant faces in 75:22.
The gloomy faces expect a crushing calamity (تَظُنُّ أَن يُفْعَلَ بِهَا فَاقِرَةٌ); it explains the fearful meaning of the expression in 75:24.
Believers' mark is on their faces from prostration (سِيمَاهُمْ فِي وُجُوهِهِمْ مِنْ أَثَرِ السُّجُودِ); this connects the section's bodily sign to a visible trace of worship.
Believing men and women have light running before them and on their right on the Day; the image gives a visible sign of the favored group.
A wall separates the believers from hypocrites, with mercy inside and punishment outside; this gives a sharp boundary between two groups on the Day, complementing 57:12's light.
God protects the righteous from that day's evil and meets them with radiance and joy (نَضْرَةً وَسُرُورًا); it joins deliverance to a visible, eased face.
The righteous are told their striving has been appreciated (وَكَانَ سَعْيُكُم مَشْكُورًا); this makes explicit why the satisfied effort in 88:9 belongs to a rewarded group.
The tranquil soul is addressed at the end of its course; the next verses say it returns pleased and pleasing, a direct inner counterpart to the section's softened, satisfied face.
The soul returns to its Lord “pleased and pleasing” (رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً); the paired رضا terms give the positive pole of the section's غضب/رضا opposition.
The pleased soul is invited among God's servants; the verse supplies the companionship side of the favored path.
The same soul is invited into the Garden, completing the return and acceptance that contrast with falling under anger.
People will be questioned that day about “the bliss” (النَّعِيمِ); the verse directly joins the section's ن ع م family to its yawm/day theme.
Musa's mother is promised that her eye will be cooled and she will not grieve (تَقَرَّ عَيْنُهَا); this is the Qur'anic bodily expression behind the section's dictionary gloss for the eye's blessing.
Musa is returned to his mother so her eye may be cooled and she not grieve; it repeats the eye-coolness phrase in the same rescue story as 20:40.
Mary is told to eat, drink, and be comforted (وَقَرِّي عَيْنًا); this is another exact Qur'anic use of eye-coolness for relief and gift.
The servants ask for spouses and children as “comfort to our eyes” (قُرَّةَ أَعْيُنٍ), tying the section's eye-coolness sense to a prayer for a blessed household and righteous leadership.
No soul knows what eye-comfort is hidden for the righteous as reward; this directly develops the section's eye-coolness gloss as an unseen good awaiting the favored.
In the Garden are what souls desire and what delights the eyes (تَلَذُّ الْأَعْيُنُ); this is a close semantic parallel to the section's cooled, content eye.
The call not to despair of God's mercy because He forgives sins gives the pardon side of the section's two outcomes.
People are told to turn to their Lord and submit before punishment comes; the verse connects repentance with avoiding the descent of the other outcome.
The command to follow the best of what was sent down before punishment arrives gives a concrete guided path, rather than mere shared religious vocabulary.
The warned person imagines regretting neglect of God's side; this is the first stated consequence of failing to respond to guidance before judgment.
The regret continues as the person admits that, had God guided them, they would have been among the mindful; it directly joins missed guidance to the rejected path.
The person imagines another chance to do good and join the righteous; it clarifies what was refused before the judgment scene.
God's answer recalls that signs came but were denied and the person was arrogant; it states the choice behind the adverse outcome.
On the Resurrection Day, those who lied about God have blackened faces; this is an exact parallel to the section's face as the mark of an outcome.
God saves the God-fearing to their place of attainment, with no evil touching them; this provides the other outcome beside the blackened faces in 39:60.
Disbelievers are driven in groups to Hell and its gates open; this explicitly stages one of two gathered communities at judgment.
The keepers ask whether messengers came with signs and the people confess; this identifies why the group in 39:71 receives that end.
The God-fearing are led in groups to the Garden, whose gates open for them; the parallel scene gives the favorable gathering opposite 39:71.
The Garden's people praise God for fulfilling His promise and giving them the land; the verse joins hamd to bestowed reward and the completed path.
On “this day,” God says He is pleased with the truthful and they with Him (رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ); the verse makes the section's two-way رضا explicit at judgment.
God is pleased with the first believers and they are pleased with Him, with gardens prepared for them; this closely identifies a community of favor through reciprocal acceptance.
The disbelievers among the People of the Book and the polytheists are named as the worst of creation and assigned the Fire; this is one side of the paired final groups.
Believers who do good are named as the best of creation; this sets the favored community against the group in 98:6.
Their reward is gardens, and God is pleased with them while they are pleased with Him; this directly completes the two-group contrast with the section's positive رضا pole.

The verse tells believers to forgive those who do not expect God's days, because He will recompense each people for what they earned; it directly uses “God's days” for the reckoning theme in the section.
Sheba is given a good land and told to eat from its Lord's provision and be grateful; this is a concrete gift-before-response scene like 20:80–81.
After Sheba turns away, a flood is sent and their gardens are replaced; the verse makes rejection of provision issue in a loss that contrasts with the granted good land.
The text identifies the punishment as recompense for their ingratitude; this completes the favor-to-punishment relation in 34:15–16.
Aad are struck by a furious wind during days of misfortune and taste humiliating punishment; this directly recalls the section's gloss of God's days as punishment coming upon Aad.
The passage asks what God did to Aad, one of the peoples explicitly named in the section's gloss of “the days of Allah.”
The same passage names Thamud and their rock-cut homes, the second people specifically named in that punishment gloss.
Pharaoh is named next among the peoples who transgressed; this adds another historical example to the section's “and others” under the days of punishment.
God pours a scourge of punishment upon those peoples (سَوْطَ عَذَابٍ); this is a particularly close image of judgment descending on a group.
The passage closes by saying the Lord is watchful; it completes the punishment scene by grounding it in divine oversight.
Thamud kill the she-camel and defy their Lord's command, then demand that punishment be brought; their chosen defiance reverses the section's picture of receiving a gift and following guidance.
The earthquake seizes the defiant Thamud immediately after 7:77; the verse gives the punishment that descends after their refusal.
The people of the Garden praise God for guiding them there (الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي هَدَانَا); it ties the section's hamd/approval word to the guided, favored path.
Abraham praises God for granting him Ishmael and Isaac in old age; this is a specific instance of hamd answering bestowed favor, the link named in the section.
The people of the Garden's final utterance is praise to God; this gives hamd as the response of those who have reached the favorable end.

The verse calls God's command to return trusts and judge justly a good instruction (نِعِمَّا يَعِظُكُم بِهِ); this is the section's secondary dictionary sense of ni'ma as a word of commendation, not a granted favor.
Believers answer a threat by saying God is sufficient for them and an excellent trustee (نِعْمَ الْوَكِيلُ); this is another explicit instance of the section's secondary ni'ma-as-praise sense.
The verse calls God an excellent protector and helper (نِعْمَ الْمَوْلَىٰ وَنِعْمَ النَّصِيرُ); this uses the section's commendatory ni'ma form for the one who gives protection.
The verse places gardens and God's approval among the promised good for the mindful; it joins bestowed reward to the رضا pole the section sets against anger.
The verse names God's pleasure as greater than the gardens promised to believers; it clarifies that favor culminates in acceptance, not material provision alone.
After the pledge at the tree, God is pleased with the believers and sends tranquility down upon them; the verse joins رضا to an embodied, descending gift.
The faithful are described as God's party, whom He supports and with whom He is pleased; this specifies a community on the accepted side of the section's division.

The believers' skins and hearts soften at God's reminder (تَلِينُ جُلُودُهُمْ وَقُلُوبُهُمْ); this is a bodily softening parallel to the section's B002 gloss for ن ع م, though the verse uses a different root.
The verse contrasts hearts humbled at God's reminder with hearts that later harden; it offers an inward counterpart to the section's outward contrast between a softened and an anger-marked face.
This verse says that when believers become angry (غَضِبُوا), they forgive; it presents a human response that interrupts anger, rather than the divine anger that descends in the section.
The righteous restrain rage and pardon people; the verse gives an ethical opposite to the bodily eruption in the section's B001 gloss for anger, using the related but different word الغيظ.
Those hostile to believers bite their fingertips from rage (الْغَيْظِ); this is a visible bodily gesture of anger, a parallel to the section's dictionary claim that anger shows itself in the body.

When one of them hears news of a daughter, his face darkens (مُسْوَدًّا); this is a different cause from divine anger, but specifically makes the face disclose an inward reaction as in the section's image.
The man hides from people in shame after his face darkens in 16:58; this clarifies the social and inward force of that visible facial sign.

When one is given the news he attributes to the Merciful, his face darkens and he suppresses anger; this is a distinct human scene where the face carries a reaction, rather than the section's divine judgment scene.
The one who seeks the Hereafter, strives for it, and believes has a recognized effort; this parallels the section's satisfied effort in 88:9, though it does not use رضا.
A person has only what he strives for; this supplies the effort side of 88:9's “pleased with her striving.”
The striving will be seen; this explains how effort becomes relevant to the satisfied judgment in 88:9.
The person will then be repaid in full; this completes the effort-and-outcome sequence related to 88:9.
The call to race toward forgiveness and a Garden prepared for the mindful gives a direct path toward the accepted outcome.
Those who remember their wrong and seek forgiveness are described as not persisting knowingly; the verse gives repentance as a route away from anger's adverse end.
Their reward is forgiveness and Gardens; this closes the sequence with the favorable end after the anger-restraint and repentance in 3:134–135, and uses ni'ma as an approving formula for the reward.

Those who believe and do good are promised high chambers and the verse calls this an excellent reward (فَنِعْمَ أَجْرُ الْعَامِلِينَ); this is the section's secondary ni'ma-as-commendation form applied to a favorable end.

The condemned are told to enter Hell and are told it is an evil abode (فَبِئْسَ مَثْوَى الْمُتَكَبِّرِينَ); this supplies the bi'sa pole paired with the section's dictionary gloss of ni'ma as praise opposite blame.
The sky becomes rose-red when split (وَرْدَةً كَالدِّهَانِ); the link to the section's B005 gloss for غضب as deep red is only a color parallel, not an anger scene.
